description:
CSE students passionate about AI, NASA data, and real-world problem solving.
We build practical, data-driven tools for smarter and more resilient farming.
Skills: AI/ML, web development, data analysis, and research.
Looking for teammates in agriculture, remote sensing, data science.
summary:
FieldShift BD is a Bangla and English farm app that helps farmers in Bangladesh decide what to grow next and when. Nearly half of Bangladesh's workers depend on farming, yet rain is unpredictable: NASA POWER data for Rajshahi shows yearly rainfall swinging from 1,015 mm to 2,080 mm, and usable monsoon rain starting anywhere from 1 April to 2 May.

A farmer saves a field (location, soil, water source, last crop) and picks a priority such as using less irrigation water or having fewer dry spells. FieldShift compares their current crops with three published BRRI crop rotations, using 25 years of NASA POWER rainfall for the area, and explains each option: why it is shown, possible benefits, risks to check locally and what is still unknown. It also offers Bangla voice questions, crop calendars, weather alerts, field reminders and leaf photo screening.

The tool supports farmer judgment; it never replaces it. Every number shows its source.
details:
What it does

FieldShift BD turns NASA Earth data into simple farm decisions in Bangla and English. A farmer adds a field with its district, soil, land type, water source and last crop; a map shows where it is. The Crop Advisor matches the field with published BARC crop zoning. The rotation comparison then sets the farmer's current crops beside three BRRI-published rotations and re-orders them by the farmer's chosen priority: less irrigation water, fewer dry spells (from NASA POWER rainfall), more crop variety for healthier soil, or published calendar dates. Every option explains why it is shown, its possible benefits, the risks to check with a local expert and what is still unknown.

The app also gives season plans and harvest windows from BRRI variety calendars, weather alerts from the forecast and recent NASA POWER data, field reminders, a farm-aware chat where farmers can ask by voice in Bangla and hear the answer read aloud, and leaf photo screening that says when it is unsure.

How it uses NASA data

We cached 25 years (2001–2025) of NASA POWER daily rainfall, temperature and solar radiation for reference points in Rajshahi, Chattogram and Dhaka. From these we compute when usable monsoon rain starts and the longest dry spells inside each crop's calendar window. These values drive the "fewer dry spells" ranking. A map in the app shows the farm, the NASA POWER reference point and its 55 × 63 km grid cell, so farmers see that the data describes their area, not one plot. GPM IMERG and SRTM samples are shown as context.

Benefits and impact

Farmers can plan with less guesswork, waste less irrigation water and lose fewer seasons. Next we plan field tests in Rajshahi and Chattogram, agronomist review of the advice, and SMAP soil moisture to reach all 64 districts.

What we considered

Honesty over hype: no invented numbers, sources shown with every result, and no option is ever chosen for the farmer. Bangla-first design, voice for farmers who prefer not to type, and an offline chat queue for weak networks.

Tools

Python, FastAPI, PostgreSQL, PyTorch, Expo/React Native (TypeScript), Docker. Data: NASA POWER, GPM IMERG, SRTM, BRRI, BARC, Open-Meteo, geoBoundaries.
